headline: High: shared write-capable, networked agent pair can leak data and corrupt shared workspaces; prompt-injection risk is lower but present via files/MCP.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Both agents can read/write files and use MCP, so attacker-controlled content can cross from one agent’s outputs into the other’s inputs through shared files or MCP artifacts. ECC’s session/files surfaces and OpenHands’ runtime files make this plausible; no provenance tracking is documented. This is more than manual copy-paste because both have automated file access.
conditions: IF the two agents share any mounted directory, workspace, or MCP-backed artifact store
IF one agent parses the other agent’s generated files as instructions or prompts
mitigations: Separate the agents onto disjoint directories
Disable MCP on the bridge path for one side
Add a manual review step before reusing generated files
Prefix imported files with provenance headers
requires-engineering: add content-sanitizing adapters between agents

B_data_leakage.rationale: ECC touches session summaries, learned skills, hooks, and security findings, while OpenHands can read files mounted into its runtime and sends context to a configured model provider. If sensitive ECC artifacts are mounted into OpenHands, leakage can occur in default workflows. The profiles do not prove a shared workspace, so I avoid high, but the pathway is real.
conditions: IF ECC artifacts are mounted into the OpenHands runtime
IF OpenHands is configured with a third-party model provider while those files contain secrets or security findings
mitigations: Mount only a minimal, scrubbed subset of files
Move secrets out of shared mounts
Rotate any exposed API keys
Review runtime mounts before launch
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss-prevention filters

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have unrestricted filesystem write, shell, subprocess, and git-state modification capabilities. ECC explicitly warns about separate roots to avoid overwriting session files, and OpenHands shares state via mounted volume only. That makes concurrent writes to the same repo or volume dangerous by default, with possible irreversible git corruption or lost work.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same repository or mounted volume
IF either agent performs git operations without external locking
mitigations: Use separate working trees
Serialize git writes with a lock file
Assign one agent read-only access
Run each agent in its own container volume
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control

D_cascading_error.rationale: ECC’s skills and session outputs can become inputs for OpenHands, which then executes shell/browser/editor actions inside its runtime. If OpenHands treats ECC-generated artifacts as authoritative, a mistaken or injected instruction can cascade into real actions. The pair therefore has a default path from generated text to executed side effects, with no documented verification gate.
conditions: IF OpenHands consumes ECC-produced files, summaries, or skills as task instructions
IF no human or automated verification step checks those inputs before execution
mitigations: Require human approval before execution
Compare generated instructions against source tasks
Restrict OpenHands to read-only dry runs first
Log and diff all imported artifacts
requires-engineering: add signed task handoff between agents

E_compliance.rationale: ECC explicitly handles security findings, session data, and hooks, while OpenHands runs with user-mounted files and third-party model-provider keys. If regulated or sensitive data is placed into OpenHands’s runtime, residency and retention obligations can diverge from ECC’s local session handling. The profiles do not show a specific HIPAA/GDPR mismatch, so medium is the highest supportable level.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into OpenHands runtime files
IF the configured model provider or runtime retention policy differs from ECC’s local session retention
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the shared runtime
Document retention settings for both agents
Use a provider with an approved DPA
Purge runtime files after each run
requires-engineering: align residency and retention controls
